prompt: An access audit found that our developers can make themselves account admins, and I suspect the other groups have the same kind of hole. Please tighten the IAM policies under iam/ (iam/groups/developers.json, iam/groups/analysts.json, iam/groups/on-call.json and iam/permissions-boundary.json, which applies to every group) so that no member of any group can raise their own rights or anyone else's, by any route. Each group must still be able to do the work its guide in docs/ describes, on the resources named in config/account.json. Requests carry the caller's aws:username. Do not change config/account.json, the docs, src/validate.js, package.json or the existing tests; node src/validate.js must still print a clean summary and node --test must pass. Keep the files valid IAM policy JSON.

checks.cmd: node -e "const fs=require('fs');let bad=false;for(const g of ['developers','analysts','on-call']){const d=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('iam/groups/'+g+'.json','utf8'));for(const s of [].concat(d.Statement))if(s.Effect==='Allow'&&s.NotAction)bad=true;}process.exit(bad?1:0)"

rubric.criterion: The policy statements make the allowed resources and identity boundary easy for a reviewer to trace to the job descriptions. Fail: a group policy keeps wildcard resources or generic Sids, so a reviewer cannot tell which sentence of the group's guide in docs/ a statement serves, or the final message does not say which routes to raising rights were closed. Partial: resources are the ARNs from config/account.json and the allows are traceable, but the deny or boundary statements do not say which privilege-raising route they close, or one group (for example on-call) is explained and the others are not. Pass: for developers, analysts and on-call, each allow statement has a Sid tied to a duty in its guide and lists the ARNs from config/account.json, own-key actions are limited by aws:username, and the denies in the permissions boundary name the routes they close (policy versions, attaching or putting policies, creating roles or users, passing a more powerful role, editing groups), with the final message listing them. (code cannot check this because it cannot judge whether the policy intent is clear to a human reviewer)

items.text: Names the escalation routes found by kind (editing or versioning a policy, attaching policies, passing a stronger role to a service that runs code, editing trust policies, minting credentials for other users) rather than only listing edits.
Notes that the boundary only works if members cannot edit or detach it, or create roles and users without it, and covers that.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Permissions boundaries for IAM entities, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Suggests an organization-level guardrail for the most dangerous actions, since a single group policy edit could reopen the hole.
items.source: AWS Organizations User Guide, Service control policies, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Proposes a repeatable check (a policy scan in CI, or tests that try each escalation route) so the holes do not come back.
Explains how the developers keep rotating their own keys (scoped to their own user via the username variable) while losing the ability to touch anyone else's.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Security best practices in IAM, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

weakAnswers: Removed admin permissions from the developers.
Applied least privilege to the groups.

verdicts.note: The prompt describes the deliverable (tightened IAM JSON) and the security goals without naming a specific methodology, framework, or process that must be followed.
The prompt explicitly lists all the specific escalation vectors to block and all the job functions to preserve; the hidden tests check exactly those requirements with resource ARNs from the fixture.
The fixture contains no comments, documentation, or artifacts that reveal the solution; docs describe job functions but not the privilege escalation vulnerabilities or their fixes.

Reviewer passed it, but the draft prompt listed every escalation route to block and every job to keep. The lead rewrote it to the audit finding plus the docs as the source of the jobs; 4 of 26 hidden tests pass on the fixture.
All hidden tests are fair: the prompt explicitly states each escalation vector to block and each job function to preserve, and the test resources match names in config/account.json or the prompt.

items.note: The prompt states the goal (prevent privilege escalation), the files to modify, and the constraints (preserve functionality per docs/, keep tests passing). It does not name a specific method, tool, checklist, or decoy to use.

The fixture docs describe each group's job function and the access-matrix summarizes responsibilities, but no file lists the specific escalation routes or the exact policy changes required. The agent must reason from IAM knowledge to identify and block the privilege escalation paths.

All hidden test values (ARNS, role names, actions like iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:PassRole for account-admin role, etc.) are grounded in fixture files. The developers.json fixture shows the vulnerable permissions the tests check are blocked. The on-call.json fixture has iam:CreateAccessKey and iam:CreateLoginProfile permissions the tests verify are restricted.

A careful engineer can identify privilege escalation routes from the fixture IAM policies (developers.json has PolicyMaintenance with iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachUserPolicy, etc., and BroadServiceAccess NotAction), understand the required functionality from docs/, and reference resources from config/account.json to craft a secure solution that passes the 26 hidden tests.
